newsitem.title: USA: Conrail hearing focuses on directors' duty.
newsitem.headline: Conrail hearing focuses on directors' duty.

text.p: Conrail Inc.'s directors breached their duty in agreeing to merge with CSX Corp., a witness said in federal court Monday, but a Conrail board member said he acted to protect the "franchise" of the railroad.

"My biggest interest was in preserving the Conrail franchise," Conrail board member H. Furlong Baldwin testified in the court hearing, at which Norfolk Southern Corp. is seeking to block Conrail's planned $8.5 billion merger with CSX.

This followed the testimony of Columbia Law School professor John Coffee, who said Conrail's board violated its corporate duties by making it difficult, if not impossible, for another company to buy Conrail.
"I think there are a number of specific respects in which they breached their fiduciary duties," Coffee said, testifying on behalf of Norfolk Southern.

Norfolk, Va.-based Norfolk Southern has sued in federal court to block the first step of the merger, a tender offer by CSX for 19.9 percent of Conrail's shares, saying Conrail improperly entered into a merger agreement with CSX that precludes the possibilities of higher offers.
Norfolk Southern has offered $110 per share cash, or $10 billion for Conrail, against the cash-and-stock offer by CSX for the Philadephia-based railroad.

Baldwin, a banker and 10-year Conrail board member, also told the court he believed Conrail's board was complying with Pennsylvania law in acting in the best interests of shareholders as well as other constituents defined by the law.
The law says company boards, when considering a merger, can also consider the interests of customers, suppliers, employees and the communities where they do business.
"No single one of these constituents should be given a disproportionate ... weight," Baldwin said.

The case is a major test of a Pennsylvania law passed after 1980s takeover battles that scarred several state corporations. The law differs from corporate law in Delaware, where many major companies are registered, which hold shareholder interests paramount when a company is being sold.
The hearing is expected to last through Tuesday.

Coffee said the Conrail board improperly agreed to continue recommending a CSX offer to buy Conrail for 270 days regardless of other bids, and agreed not to amend its "poison pill" anti-takeover provisions for any offer other than Richmond, Va.-based CSX's.

Furthermore, he said, Conrail agreed to a structure of the bid that would effectively enable CSX to gain control of Conrail once it has succeeded with its initial tender offer, which expires Wednesday.
"The merger will be a 'fait accompli'," Coffee said, arguing that a 19.9 percent CSX stake will effectively stampede other investors into approving the rest of the deal.
Some takeover stock specialists have said that unless CSX increases its offer, shareholders at a December meeting will defeat a waiver in Conrail's charter designed to allow the deal to proceed.

Called to the witness stand by Norfolk Southern, Baldwin said Conrail began pursuing a merger with CSX after a September board retreat where a number of strategic options, including a combination with Norfolk Southern, were considered.

Under questioning over the extent to which Conrail considered interests other than those of shareholders, Baldwin acknowledged a merger with CSX would produce greater near-term overhead reductions -- a term Norfolk Southern's attorney defined as "layoffs" -- than a merger with Norfolk Southern.

But he said over the long term a Conrail-CSX combination would have more workers than the two firms do now. He also said no consideration was given to specific communities that might be affected by overlap between the two firms.

Baldwin had difficulty describing specific points of "lock-up" provisions and other measures designed to cement the Conrail-CSX deal that are contested by Norfolk Southern but he said directors had been meticulous in seeking assurances from attorneys that the deal complied with all applicable laws.
And he insisted that the board's approval of the deal reflected sound business judgment, which Conrail has argued in court papers cannot be second-guessed by a court.
"I understood very well what I needed to know to make the business judgments that were my responsibility," Baldwin said. "I am very comfortable with the business decision."
